discussions.strategist:
Most of today's list is filler: a Mexican distributor tie-up, a caiman study, a Libyan tender, a mine-safety course. Five items matter.

Freeport is the big one. Mining.com now names the Bagdad copper expansion and says Freeport "approves" US$4.5bn for it. Bagdad is, as I understand it, Freeport's Arizona copper operation (background knowledge, not in the material). On 4 November the Arizona story had no named mine and no FID. The naming is progress, but the verb is a headline's, not a filing's. My Freeport prediction still needs Freeport's own release stating the decision and the capex. Grasberg tonnage also remains open.

Costs run through three stories. Mining.com's "copper's biggest new mine stumbles again as costs soar" fits my 17 October view that costs matter more than prices. The headline names no mine, so I won't attach it to any project. Agnico and Vale warning of an Ontario labour squeeze belongs beside Alamos's Island Gold shaft delay. I've treated those as correlated risks, not cause and effect, and labour pressure joins I-80's Nevada labour story as a theme to track.

Permits and critical minerals form the third group. B2Gold's US$740M Gramalote faces a key permit test. Colombia's repeal still has no decree in the record, so this is the first concrete test of the "5.3M hectares" story, and I'd like the decision and its scope before drawing any supply read. On the other side, CNBC reports China expanding overseas mining stakes, which tightens its grip on critical minerals. Mining.com also says Western tungsten prices nearly quadruple China's. That is a spread with no prices, dates or source, so it stays unscored.

The Democrats' win puts US mining policy under scrutiny. That is a watch item. Permitting is where policy shows up in supply, and nothing here is measurable yet.

Not worth time: the Sandvik–Eldorado equipment support deal doesn't change Eldorado's unverified 18% cut, and Rare Earths Norway's US$27M Fen pilot plant is a pilot, not supply.

PREDICTION: B2Gold publishes a company release or exchange notice stating the outcome of the Gramalote permit review | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
PREDICTION: A named wire service or Mining.com publishes a numeric tungsten price in US dollars per metric ton for both Western and Chinese delivery in the same report | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
discussions.geologist:
Colleagues, most of today's batch is sentiment and thin sourcing, but a few items touch threads we're tracking.

Freeport is the main one. Two Mining.com items (7 and 13, the same story) say Freeport "approves" a US$4.5 billion Bagdad copper expansion. That's the first time the Arizona expansion has a name attached. It doesn't settle our question yet. Our standard is a company statement of a final investment decision, and "approves" in a trade headline could mean board sign-off, a permit step, or financing. From background knowledge, Bagdad is Freeport's Arizona copper-molybdenum operation, so the name fits, but that isn't sourced here. Keep it separate from the US$504M "bought rather than built" Arizona story, which has an unnamed buyer and a different asset. I'd move the naming part of our Freeport predictions to partly supported and keep the FID question open until the release is in hand.

B2Gold's US$740M Gramalote faces a "key permit test" (Mining.com). The headline doesn't say which permit or what the test is. Gramalote is, from background knowledge, a Colombian project, and the Colombia repeal "opening 5.3M ha" is still a single-aggregator figure. Don't link them until B2Gold or the regulator says so.

Agnico and Vale warn of an Ontario labour squeeze (Northern Miner). That's the same region where Alamos's Island Gold shaft is slipping and Gold Fields' Windfall is waiting on an unnamed hurdle. Treat these as correlated pressures, not proven cause. In my experience, labour squeezes show up first as deferred drilling and slower development, and that's cost per tonne, not output.

"Copper's biggest new mine stumbles again as costs soar" (Mining.com) doesn't name the mine. I won't attach it to Oyu Tolgoi without the operator's wording. It's a cost signal consistent with our cost-over-price view, with no tonnes.

Smaller items: Rare Earths Norway's approval of a $27 million Fen pilot plant is a real capital figure, but it's pilot scale, so it's a milestone, not supply. The "nearly quadruple" tungsten price comparison is a regional spread with no stated base. China's overseas stakes (CNBC) fits our Congo governance thread, and the Democrats' win story is policy framing, not an award.

PREDICTION: B2Gold publishes a company release or filing stating the outcome of the Gramalote permit review | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
PREDICTION: Rare Earths Norway publishes a company release confirming the start of pilot plant commissioning at Fen | BY: 2027-06-30 | CONFIDENCE: low
discussions.strategist_reply:
Yukon, your point on the Freeport wording is the one I'd underline. "Approves" in a trade headline could mean board sign-off, a permit step or financing, and I was too quick to read the Bagdad naming as progress toward an FID. I now rate it partly supported: the asset is named, the decision isn't. Your Gramalote caution also holds. A "key permit test" with no permit named doesn't connect to the 5.3M ha repeal until B2Gold or the regulator says so.

Your expertise sharpens my view on Ontario. Deferred drilling is the first casualty of a labour squeeze, which makes exploration budgets a better early signal than production or cost-per-tonne lines. I'll watch for that.

Where I'd push back: the unnamed copper mine's cost overrun deserves more weight than you give it. Leaving it unattached is right, but a cost theme across several projects matters even without a name.

What we may both have missed: the CNBC overseas-stakes story is about who controls offtake and permitting abroad. For Western equity valuations, that could matter more than any single mine. Also, the Democrats' win is a 2027 permitting question, not a November one. Permitting changes take quarters to reach supply.

Updated predictions:

discussions.geologist_reply:

I'd push back on one point. You call the Gramalote review "the first concrete test" of the Colombian "5.3M hectares" story. I'd hold the line. The headline doesn't name the permit, and nothing in the record ties it to the repeal. If B2Gold's release makes that link, we can revisit. Until then it's a Gramalote permit, not a supply signal.

On labour, I agree the Ontario warning and Nevada's I-80 story are a theme. I'd add that labour pressure shows up first in cost per tonne, so Island Gold and Windfall belong in unit-cost guidance, not headline output.

What we both missed: the Freeport Bagdad story ran twice on Mining.com (items 7 and 13). That's one story, not corroboration. We should count sources, not repeats.

discussions.summary:
**Key stories:**
- Mining.com reports Freeport's US$4.5bn Bagdad copper expansion, which appeared twice but is one story. The asset is named, but "approves" doesn't establish a final investment decision.
- B2Gold's US$740M Gramalote faces an unnamed "key permit test." Neither side links it to Colombia's repeal, which is sourced to a single aggregator.
- Agnico and Vale warn of an Ontario labour squeeze, alongside Alamos's Island Gold shaft delay and Gold Fields' Windfall timing.
- An unnamed copper mine's cost overrun, a tungsten price spread with no prices or dates, CNBC on Chinese overseas mining stakes, and the Democrats' win as a policy watch item.

**Where they agree:**
- Most of the batch is filler or thinly sourced.
- The Bagdad naming is progress, but not an FID.
- The Ontario items are correlated pressures, not proven cause.
- The unnamed cost overrun shouldn't be attached to any project.
- Fen is a pilot milestone, not supply.

**Where they disagree:**
- **Gramalote:** Meldrum initially called the review the first concrete test of the 5.3M ha story. Yukon Cornelius holds that the permit is unnamed and unlinked, so it isn't a supply signal until B2Gold or the regulator makes the connection.
- **Cost overrun:** Meldrum says a cost theme across projects matters even without a name. Yukon Cornelius treats it as a cost signal with no tonnage.
- **Early labour indicator:** Yukon Cornelius expects pressure to show first in unit costs. Meldrum prefers exploration budgets, such as deferred drilling.
- **Gramalote wording:** Meldrum's prediction says "release or filing"; Yukon Cornelius's says "release or exchange notice."
